sections.h2: Three offices behind a Franklin County bill
sections.html:
Franklin County sits in the northwestern Panhandle and has more than 11,000 residents. Outside the cities of Apalachicola and Carrabelle, the county commission serves as the local government. Those two cities, the commission and the school board set the rates.

The tax work is split three ways: the appraiser puts a value on the parcel, the tax collector sends the bill, and the clerk of court handles any tax deed auction. Know which desk to call and you save time.

  • Property appraiser: keeps the roll, takes exemption filings and mails TRIM notices in August. It neither sets rates nor collects tax.
  • Tax collector: 33 Market Street, Suite 202, Apalachicola; (850) 653-9323. Prints bills, accepts payment, sells certificates.
  • Clerk: holds the courthouse auction of tax deeds and records your deed when you sell.

Exemption paperwork comes early in the year and the bill comes last.

Franklin County property tax steps
WhenStepOffice
January 1 to March 1Window for homestead and agricultural classification filingsProperty appraiser
April 1Business personal property returns dueProperty appraiser
AugustTRIM notice, marked as a notice and not a billProperty appraiser
By November 1Statements mailedTax collector
November through FebruaryDiscount slides from 4% to 1%Tax collector
April 1 of the next yearReal estate bill late; 3% penaltyTax collector
On or before June 1Online lien auction for unpaid parcelsTax collector

The TRIM notice is not a bill, even though it comes in the mail. Wait for the November statement before you pay.

The tax collector posts a millage table, written as decimals. A millage figure is the tax per thousand dollars of taxable value. The lines below are the 2025 figures, so ask the collector for the table covering the current year before relying on them.

  • County: .00504590
  • School, local effort: .00194400
  • School, discretionary: .00224800
  • Northwest Florida Water Management: .00002070
  • Carrabelle: .00750000
  • Apalachicola: .00834570
  • Dog Island: .00400000
  • Eastpoint district: .00375000
  • Alligator Point: .00123040

Only one local line fits a given address. Carrabelle and Apalachicola are the two cities, while Eastpoint, Dog Island and Alligator Point appear as districts. County, school and water lines stack on top. Flat assessments for services print on the same statement, so read the lower part of the bill too.

Florida's homestead exemption takes up to $50,000 off the value of a home you live in permanently. The appraiser accepts applications from January 1 through March 1. Once you start renting the house out, eligibility is gone.

Once a homestead is in place, a statutory cap limits how fast its assessed value can rise. A sale wipes out that cushion for the next owner, so your buyer's first Franklin County bill may look much larger than yours did. If you plan to move to another Florida home, ask the appraiser there whether part of your cap can carry over.

Gather what the appraiser will want before you visit: a photo ID, proof that you live in the home, and a copy of your deed. A quick call to the office beforehand can spare you a second trip.

State law lets you prepay in quarterly installments under s. 197.222 if you apply to the tax collector by May 1 of the assessment year. Low-income homestead owners can also defer part of the tax with Form DR-570 by March 31. Whether either one helps depends on your income and timing, so call the collector at (850) 653-9323 before the dates pass. Lenders that escrow normally pay the bill themselves. Selling mid-plan? Say so to the closing agent, so any installment still owing is paid at the table instead of falling to the buyer.

sections.h2: After April 1 on an unpaid parcel
sections.html:
Real estate bills pick up a 3 percent penalty as April begins. Come May, the parcel appears in the newspaper for three weeks running, and the owner pays for the ad. Business equipment and mobile home attachments follow a rougher path of monthly interest and warrants.

Around the end of May the collector auctions a lien certificate online. Bidders start at 18 percent and bid the rate down, and the lowest rate wins. The winner pays your tax and holds a lien, and you owe them the bid rate. A buyer cannot take your house at that point. A deed application is allowed two years after April 1 of the issue year, and a certificate left unredeemed for 22 months can end in a deed sale.

Homestead parcels owing under $250 are not offered to the public. The county holds those at 18 percent a year until the total passes $250.

sections.h2: How a tax deed sale works
sections.html:
The clerk's office runs the sale. When sales are scheduled, they are generally held on the first Monday of the month at 11:00 AM inside the main courthouse at 33 Market Street, Apalachicola. Call the clerk to verify before attending. Notice runs in the Apalachicola Times once a week for four weeks.

  • You can redeem by paying the tax collector before the sale, or before the clerk receives the winning bidder's full payment.
  • For homestead property, the opening bid adds half of the latest assessed value to the taxes, interest and fees.
  • The winning bidder posts a nonrefundable deposit of 5 percent or $200, whichever is greater, and pays the balance within 24 hours.
  • Documentary stamps of $.70 per $100 of the bid and recording fees are due from the bidder.
  • Some government liens survive the deed, and every property is sold as is.

Most title insurers want a quiet title lawsuit before they will insure a tax deed property, and the deed gives the buyer a right to immediate possession even though legal action may still be needed to get it. For an owner the lesson is simple: a sale you close before the auction date avoids all of that, and your own buyer gets a normal title search.

An unpaid balance is a lien that the buyer's title company will insist on clearing. The closing agent can send the payoff to the tax collector from your proceeds. Ask for a figure good through the closing day, since a bill past April 1 grows by a 3 percent penalty and newspaper advertising.

The state also taxes the deed itself. Documentary stamps run 70 cents on each $100 of consideration outside Miami-Dade, and every party to the document is liable. The clerk takes the payment at recording.

Bring your ID, your deed and your latest tax bill to the title agent, and read the draft settlement statement before you sign. A cash buyer can often close faster, which helps if a sale date or the April 1 penalty is near.

faqs.q: Which month is the cheapest to pay in Franklin County?
faqs.a: November. The tax collector prints a 4 percent discount for November, 3 percent for December, 2 percent for January and 1 percent for February.

faqs.q: Does the appraiser or the collector set my rate?
faqs.a: Neither. The appraiser does not set rates, and the rates come from the county commission, school board and each city or district.

faqs.q: Is a house with a tax certificate on it still sellable?
faqs.a: Yes. Closing pays the redemption to the tax collector, which then repays the certificate holder. Ask (850) 653-9323 for the redemption total.

faqs.q: When is the Franklin County exemption filing cutoff?
faqs.a: March 1. Filing opens January 1, and the home must be your permanent residence.

faqs.q: How fast can a tax deed auction happen?
faqs.a: Slowly. A certificate holder waits two years after April 1 of the issue year to apply, and you can redeem up to the point the clerk receives the winning bidder's full payment.
